Arya Nagarjuna's dedication of the virtue created by this composition A Topical Listing of the Writings of Arya Nagarjuna We created this listing of the works of Arya Nagarjuna as more of a biographical exercise, than a definitive, bibliographical one. It is based primarily on three versions of the Tengyur, or collections of traditional Tibetan translations of some 3600 classical commentaries from ancient India: the Derge (widely considered the most authoritative); the Sertri ("gold calligraphy," perhaps older); and the Nartang (a solid alternative edition). We did not attempt a close analysis of additional versions of the Tengyur; and it may be that there are a few other authentic works by Arya Nagarjuna to be found there. We have not generally included works by The Arya which are reported but not actually found in these editions of the Tengyur. In some case the attribution of works to Nagarjuna is questioned by the extremely careful & competent compilers of the various Tengyurs; it was a common corruption in ancient times to say something like "my book is so good, it may as well have been written by Nagarjuna"-and then in time the book would actually be credited to him. We have studied these cases in the ancient catalogs, and we agree fully with these compilers' opinions, and have not included those particular titles. We have relied most heavily upon the truly masterful ancient native Tibetan catalog to the Derge edition. The works in the Derge Tengyur have been very admirably listed and analyzed by the creators of the great Tohoku University Catalog of this collection, and we have relied heavily upon their work. We have also availed ourselves of the fine work of Professor Lokesh Chandra in bringing the often corrupt Tibetanized Sanskrit titles into order. The number of folios in the works are patchy in the originals and may be off by one or two pages, but not more-and so they give a good idea of the relative size of each title; although of course with Arya Nagarjuna a work of 20 folios can change the history of a continent for the next 2,000 years. In some cases the same work may be referred to by different names in different editions of the Tengyur; we have tried to avoid listing both titles but a few cases may have snuck in. We have not re-created Sanskrit titles, as we consider this an inexact and potentially misleading exercise; where a title is not mentioned in situ, we have noted that fact. The translations of the titles into English is by the two translators of the present volume. We have broken the titles down into subject categories, according to our judgement and a quick review of the contents of works. In ordering them, we generally follow the lead of the native creators of the Derge Tengyur. These categories may perhaps be polished in time, but for now are very indicative of topics that The Arya considered important; which is the purpose of the exercise for our present volume. Arya Nagarjuna's dedication of the virtue created by this composition A Topical Listing of the Writings of Arya Nagarjuna We created this listing of the works of Arya Nagarjuna as more of a biographical exercise, than a definitive, bibliographical one. It is based primarily on three versions of the Tengyur, or collections of traditional Tibetan translations of some 3600 classical commentaries from ancient India: the Derge (widely considered the most authoritative); the Sertri ("gold calligraphy," perhaps older); and the Nartang (a solid alternative edition). We did not attempt a close analysis of additional versions of the Tengyur; and it may be that there are a few other authentic works by Arya Nagarjuna to be found there. We have not generally included works by The Arya which are reported but not actually found in these editions of the Tengyur. In some case the attribution of works to Nagarjuna is questioned by the extremely careful & competent compilers of the various Tengyurs; it was a common corruption in ancient times to say something like "my book is so good, it may as well have been written by Nagarjuna"-and then in time the book would actually be credited to him. We have studied these cases in the ancient catalogs, and we agree fully with these compilers' opinions, and have not included those particular titles. We have relied most heavily upon the truly masterful ancient native Tibetan catalog to the Derge edition. The works in the Derge Tengyur have been very admirably listed and analyzed by the creators of the great Tohoku University Catalog of this collection, and we have relied heavily upon their work. We have also availed ourselves of the fine work of Professor Lokesh Chandra in bringing the often corrupt Tibetanized Sanskrit titles into order. The number of folios in the works are patchy in the originals and may be off by one or two pages, but not more-and so they give a good idea of the relative size of each title; although of course with Arya Nagarjuna a work of 20 folios can change the history of a continent for the next 2,000 years. In some cases the same work may be referred to by different names in different editions of the Tengyur; we have tried to avoid listing both titles but a few cases may have snuck in. We have not re-created Sanskrit titles, as we consider this an inexact and potentially misleading exercise; where a title is not mentioned in situ, we have noted that fact. The translations of the titles into English is by the two translators of the present volume. We have broken the titles down into subject categories, according to our judgement and a quick review of the contents of works. In ordering them, we generally follow the lead of the native creators of the Derge Tengyur. These categories may perhaps be polished in time, but for now are very indicative of topics that The Arya considered important; which is the purpose of the exercise for our present volume. Arya Nagarjuna's dedication of the virtue created by this composition A Topical Listing of the Writings of Arya Nagarjuna We created this listing of the works of Arya Nagarjuna as more of a biographical exercise, than a definitive, bibliographical one. It is based primarily on three versions of the Tengyur, or collections of traditional Tibetan translations of some 3600 classical commentaries from ancient India: the Derge (widely considered the most authoritative); the Sertri ("gold calligraphy," perhaps older); and the Nartang (a solid alternative edition). We did not attempt a close analysis of additional versions of the Tengyur; and it may be that there are a few other authentic works by Arya Nagarjuna to be found there. We have not generally included works by The Arya which are reported but not actually found in these editions of the Tengyur. In some case the attribution of works to Nagarjuna is questioned by the extremely careful & competent compilers of the various Tengyurs; it was a common corruption in ancient times to say something like "my book is so good, it may as well have been written by Nagarjuna"-and then in time the book would actually be credited to him. We have studied these cases in the ancient catalogs, and we agree fully with these compilers' opinions, and have not included those particular titles. We have relied most heavily upon the truly masterful ancient native Tibetan catalog to the Derge edition. The works in the Derge Tengyur have been very admirably listed and analyzed by the creators of the great Tohoku University Catalog of this collection, and we have relied heavily upon their work. We have also availed ourselves of the fine work of Professor Lokesh Chandra in bringing the often corrupt Tibetanized Sanskrit titles into order. The number of folios in the works are patchy in the originals and may be off by one or two pages, but not more-and so they give a good idea of the relative size of each title; although of course with Arya Nagarjuna a work of 20 folios can change the history of a continent for the next 2,000 years. In some cases the same work may be referred to by different names in different editions of the Tengyur; we have tried to avoid listing both titles but a few cases may have snuck in. We have not re-created Sanskrit titles, as we consider this an inexact and potentially misleading exercise; where a title is not mentioned in situ, we have noted that fact. The translations of the titles into English is by the two translators of the present volume. We have broken the titles down into subject categories, according to our judgement and a quick review of the contents of works. In ordering them, we generally follow the lead of the native creators of the Derge Tengyur. Do the parties in a debate ever perceive the same object? The fourth distinction in the above list addresses whether or not two parties in a debate can ever be perceiving exactly the same object under consideration. Gyaltsab Je, in the present work, mentions that this question is a criterion that we must use for establishing whether or not an independently effective reason (the first item in his list) can exist. He then goes on to describe how some say that Master Bhavaviveka, hailed as the founder of the Independent Group, denies that there could be a common subject that can be discussed logically in the context of examining suchness; and how that is in direct contradiction to the idea that a reason could have some power of its own. It would appear that the idea which is being attributed to Master Bhavaviveka has its roots in a famous debate that he put forth some 1500 years ago, where he tries to clarify the meaning of the opening lines of Arya Nagarjuna's Wisdom. Here first is a presentation of Master Chandrakirti's famous refutation of Master Bhavaviveka's arguments, as given by the great Mongol scholar Chujey Ngawang Pelden in his commentary upon the wording of Entering the Middle Way. The focus of this discussion is the use of the expression "in an ultimate sense" as a qualifier in a proof that the sense powers cannot start on their own. Arya Nagarjuna's dedication of the virtue created by this composition A Topical Listing of the Writings of Arya Nagarjuna We created this listing of the works of Arya Nagarjuna as more of a biographical exercise, than a definitive, bibliographical one. It is based primarily on three versions of the Tengyur, or collections of traditional Tibetan translations of some 3600 classical commentaries from ancient India: the Derge (widely considered the most authoritative); the Sertri ("gold calligraphy," perhaps older); and the Nartang (a solid alternative edition). We did not attempt a close analysis of additional versions of the Tengyur; and it may be that there are a few other authentic works by Arya Nagarjuna to be found there. We have not generally included works by The Arya which are reported but not actually found in these editions of the Tengyur. In some case the attribution of works to Nagarjuna is questioned by the extremely careful & competent compilers of the various Tengyurs; it was a common corruption in ancient times to say something like "my book is so good, it may as well have been written by Nagarjuna"-and then in time the book would actually be credited to him. We have studied these cases in the ancient catalogs, and we agree fully with these compilers' opinions, and have not included those particular titles. We have relied most heavily upon the truly masterful ancient native Tibetan catalog to the Derge edition. The works in the Derge Tengyur have been very admirably listed and analyzed by the creators of the great Tohoku University Catalog of this collection, and we have relied heavily upon their work. We have also availed ourselves of the fine work of Professor Lokesh Chandra in bringing the often corrupt Tibetanized Sanskrit titles into order. The number of folios in the works are patchy in the originals and may be off by one or two pages, but not more-and so they give a good idea of the relative size of each title; although of course with Arya Nagarjuna a work of 20 folios can change the history of a continent for the next 2,000 years. In some cases the same work may be referred to by different names in different editions of the Tengyur; we have tried to avoid listing both titles but a few cases may have snuck in. We have not re-created Sanskrit titles, as we consider this an inexact and potentially misleading exercise; where a title is not mentioned in situ, we have noted that fact. The translations of the titles into English is by the two translators of the present volume. We have broken the titles down into subject categories, according to our judgement and a quick review of the contents of works. In ordering them, we generally follow the lead of the native creators of the Derge Tengyur. These categories may perhaps be polished in time, but for now are very indicative of topics that The Arya considered important; which is the purpose of the exercise for our present volume.
